query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A single integrated thermo-mechanical treatment—specifically cryogenic rolling followed by a carefully controlled, low‐temperature annealing—is expected to modify the lamellar microstructure of the eutectic HEA. This treatment should refine the grain structure and promote the formation of more coherent, nanoscale‐decorated phase boundaries that can arrest dislocation pile-ups, thereby mitigating the stress concentrations responsible for microcracking while retaining or even boosting the alloy’s strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase (L12 and B2) lamellar colony microstructure in which semi‐coherent internal boundaries are prone to intense dislocation storage and local stress concentrations that lead to brittle failure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Cryogenic rolling (to induce severe plastic deformation at low temperatures) followed by a tailored low-temperature annealing treatment that promotes limited recovery and nanocrystallization at the phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile conditions with standard strain rates; process parameters (e.g., cryo-rolling strain and annealing temperature/time) optimized to retain the lamellar architecture with modified interphase boundary characteristics.
generation.structural_mediator: A more refined, dual-scale heterogeneous microstructure featuring ultrafine recrystallized L12 domains and partially recovered, nano-structured B2 regions with enhanced and more chemically homogeneous (preferably more coherent) interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling increases stored dislocation density predominantly in the ductile L12 phase while reducing dynamic recovery in the B2 phase. The subsequent low-temperature annealing then selectively promotes controlled recovery and nanocrystallization at the phase boundaries, leading to modified interfaces that are capable of deflecting or arresting further dislocation motion. This combination reduces the localized pile-ups that generate stress concentrations and microcracks and also builds up beneficial back-stress hardening that simultaneously enhances strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the treated HEA will exhibit notably improved room-temperature ductility (i.e. increased elongation to failure) while maintaining or increasing the yield and ultimate tensile strengths, thus overcoming the intrinsic brittleness and limited tensile ductility caused by dislocation accumulation at internal boundaries.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies that suffers from dislocation pile-ups at semi-coherent B2/L12 boundaries, resulting in microcracking and a poor strength-ductility balance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is primarily expected to be effective under quasi-static, room-temperature tensile loading; its efficacy at very high strain rates or elevated temperatures is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., those reported in PMC5818523 and PMC6353877) have independently shown that cryo-rolling plus annealing can enhance strength and ductility via microstructural refinement, extrapolating this to explicitly modify dislocation-blocking phase boundaries in a lamellar eutectic HEA is a novel application. The exact kinetics of nano-precipitate formation and the degree to which the interphase boundary coherence is improved remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic HEA specimens. Subject one set to the cryogenic rolling plus controlled low-temperature annealing treatment and leave the other set untreated. Conduct standard room-temperature tensile tests while using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to characterize the dislocation distributions and the chemistry and coherence of the phase boundaries in both sets.
measurements: Dislocation density and distribution at phase boundaries (via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in ductility (e.g., improvement in elongation of at least 10% relative to the baseline) accompanying either maintained or increased strength, and if microstructural analysis does not reveal a clear reduction in dislocation pile-ups at the interface (or improvement in boundary coherence), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Given the energy-efficient improvement and large safety factors, the attainment of high strength and high ductility in materials is arguably a vital requirement for most engineering applications. Unfortunately, these two properties are generally mutually exclusive, particularly in pure metals and alloys. Eutectic alloys specifically exhibit good liquidity and castability, preventing common casting flaws, like internal shrinkage and compositional segregation, to downgrade mechanical properties. They also possess a regularly arranged lamellar organization that can be viewed as a natural or in situ composite, which enables synergetic reinforcement to improve mechanical properties and sometimes bring unusual electrical, magnetic, and optical behaviors. Eutectic materials have therefore been investigated in diverse application fields, but traditionally, only certain eutectic systems have been of major commercial importance. Recently, eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), first proposed by Lu et al. in 2014, were designed based on the above eutectic-alloy concept.
